title: Copied by the King's Men
sum: A new heading opens the fifth collection of Proverbs: more sayings of Solomon, "which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied" (25:1). It is the only place in the Bible that names a group of scribes and dates their work, to the reign of Hezekiah, about 715–687 BC. The chapter that follows reads like a lesson for young men at court: how kings search out matters (25:2–5), how to behave in the royal presence (25:6–7), how to handle a dispute (25:8–10), and the power of a well-timed word (25:11–15).

The second half is a gallery of pictures from daily life: honey, snow at harvest, rainless clouds, a broken tooth, vinegar on soda, a leaking roof, a trampled spring, a city with its wall breached. In the middle stands the most famous saying of the chapter: feed the one who hates you, "for you will be scooping up burning coals onto his head" (25:22), the saying Paul quotes in Romans 12:20.
readings: Read as a court handbook

Glendon Bryce and Raymond Van Leeuwen argued that 25:2–27 is a small, planned "book" of instruction, framed by "glory" and "searching" in 25:2 and 25:27. It moves from the king (25:2–5) to the courtier (25:6–15) and then to life among neighbors and enemies (25:16–27). On this reading Hezekiah's scribes did more than copy: they arranged old sayings to train officials.
Read as a collection of pictures

Most of the chapter's sayings are comparisons with no "like" or "so": two images set side by side, and the reader is left to see the link ("Clouds and wind, and yet no rain: / that is someone who boasts of a gift that is a lie", 25:14). Read this way, the chapter trains the eye. Wisdom is learning to notice how the world works and to see one's own conduct in it.

views.H: The heading places the collection in Hezekiah's reign, a time of religious reform, of refugees from the fallen northern kingdom, and of growing literacy in Judah. Kings and Chronicles present Hezekiah as a new David and Solomon (2 Kings 18:3–5; 2 Chronicles 29:30; 2 Chronicles 30:26), and gathering Solomon's sayings fits that program. The court setting shows in the sayings about kings, nobles, messengers and lawsuits.
views.C: Most critical scholars accept the heading as a plausible memory of real scribal activity in the late 700s BC, though the sayings themselves may be older or younger than Hezekiah. Several sayings repeat ones in 10:1–22:16 (25:24 = 21:9), which suggests a separate source. The witnesses checked for this part: the Leningrad Codex with its Ketiv and Qere; the Greek in Rahlfs' edition, with Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus and his notes on Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus for single-codex readings; and the SBL Greek New Testament for Romans 12:20 and 2 Peter 2:22. The Syriac, the Targum and Jerome's Latin are cited only as reported by the sources named. In the Greek, chapters 25–29 come after 30:1–14, 24:23–34, 30:15–33 and 31:1–9, and the Greek adds lines at 25:10 and 25:20.
views.W: Court wisdom was an international genre. Egyptian instructions such as Ptahhotep and Amenemope teach officials how to behave before superiors, and the Aramaic Words of Ahiqar, set at the Assyrian court in Hezekiah's own era, has a close parallel to 25:15. In chapter 2 of Amenemope the "heated man" has fallen into the water, and the reader is told to pull him out: "Fill his belly with bread of your own, / That he be sated and weep" (as Lichtheim translates it). Many compare it with 25:21–22.
views.J: The Talmud credits "Hezekiah and his company" with writing down Proverbs (Bava Batra 15a). Rabbinic readers applied 25:21–22 to the evil inclination, the enemy within, to be fed with the bread and water of Torah (Sukkah 52a), and Maimonides made 25:11 his key to the levels of meaning in Scripture.
views.X: Paul's quotation of 25:21–22 in Romans 12:20, together with Jesus' command to love enemies, made these verses central to Christian ethics of nonretaliation. Jesus' advice to take the lowest seat (Luke 14:8–11) echoes 25:6–7. Augustine read the coals as the burning pain of repentance, a reading most Christians have followed.

deep.b:
The saying asks something hard: if the one who hates you is hungry, feed him; if thirsty, give him water. Israel's law already required help for an enemy's ox or donkey (Exodus 23:4–5), and Proverbs forbids gloating and revenge (24:17–18; 24:29). This goes further, to personal kindness. The reason given is strange: "you will be scooping up burning coals onto his head." The verb chotheh means scooping or carrying fire, as from a hearth; the familiar "heap" is the Greek translator's word.

Four main readings exist. (1) Burning shame: kindness makes the enemy feel his guilt so keenly that he repents. Augustine called the coals "burning groans of repentance", and this is the majority Christian view. (2) Added judgment: if he does not repent, your kindness will add to God's judgment on him; coals elsewhere signal wrath (Psalm 140:10). Some church fathers, including Chrysostom, mentioned this reading while insisting that the goal was reconciliation. (3) A rite of repentance: Siegfried Morenz pointed to an Egyptian Demotic tale where a penitent carries a pan of burning coals on his head as a public sign of remorse. If the saying draws on such a custom, kindness leads the enemy to show repentance. William Klassen weighed the readings and favored a sign of repentance. (4) Rabbinic: the Talmud (Sukkah 52a) applies the verse to the evil inclination and reads the last word as "he will make him at peace with you".

Paul quotes the Greek of 25:21–22 closely (Romans 12:20), with a different verb for "feed" (psomize, the reading of Codex Vaticanus, where the Greek has trephe), and frames it with "do not avenge yourselves" (Romans 12:19) and "conquer evil with good" (Romans 12:21). He leaves out the promise that the Lord will repay you. In context the point is not a clever way to punish an enemy but a way to end the cycle of evil. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope has a similar counsel about rescuing the "heated man" who has fallen into the water: "Fill his belly with bread of your own, / That he be sated and weep" (chapter 2, as Lichtheim translates it).

"Copied" (he'tiqu) means "moved, transferred". It is the vocabulary of scribes moving texts from one scroll to another or from memory to writing. Hezekiah's court had a secretary, Shebna, and a recorder, Joah (2 Kings 18:18), and the king is remembered for reorganizing worship, storehouses and records (2 Chronicles 29–31; 2 Chronicles 32:27–30). The repeated sayings in 25–29 (25:24 = 21:9; 26:22 = 18:8; 27:13 = 20:16; 28:6 and 19:1) show that the men of Hezekiah did not check their new collection against the older one, or chose to keep both. The arrangement shows editorial care: sayings are grouped by catchword and theme (fools in 26:1–12, the lazy one in 26:13–16, the righteous and wicked in 28–29), and 25:2–27 seems to have its own frame.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the scribes describe their own work
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The first saying after the heading is "The glory of God is to keep a matter hidden, / and the glory of kings is searching a matter out" (25:2). If Hezekiah's men chose to open their collection with it, they may have meant it as a description of what they themselves were doing as the king's men: searching out Solomon's sayings and bringing them to light. The unit then closes with "searching out their glory" (25:27). I have not found this exact reading in the commentaries I know, though Bryce and Van Leeuwen note the frame and its royal setting. It cannot be proved, and the saying stands on its own without it.

echoes: 1 Kings 4:32; 2 Kings 18:1–8; 2 Kings 18:18; 2 Chronicles 29:30; Exodus 20:16; Exodus 23:4–5; Luke 14:8–11; Romans 12:20; Matthew 5:44; Jude 12; 21:9; 16:32

settings.what: The heading of the Hezekiah collection
settings.by: The editors of Proverbs, naming Solomon as source and Hezekiah's officials as copyists
settings.to: Readers of the growing book, first at the royal court of Judah
settings.when: In the reign of Hezekiah king of Judah, about 715–687 BC, after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC
settings.why: The heading tells readers where the sayings came from and who handed them on. It claims Solomon's authority for the sayings while admitting a later stage of collecting. Knowing this keeps readers from imagining Solomon writing every line, and shows Proverbs as a book that grew through generations of careful scribes.
settings.readers: Later Jewish readers, living without a king of their own, kept the heading as a memory of the royal scribes. The Talmud expanded it into a whole account of "Hezekiah and his company" writing down Proverbs, Isaiah, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes (Bava Batra 15a). The Greek translator turned "men" into "friends", the court title of his own Hellenistic world.
views: Most scholars, critical and traditional, take the heading as a real memory of scribal work at Hezekiah's court.
Some think the heading was added later to give the collection a royal pedigree, as headings in Psalms were.

settings.what: Sayings for the king's court and for life among neighbors
settings.by: The sages of Solomon's tradition, as collected by Hezekiah's scribes
settings.to: Young men being trained for service at court: future officials, messengers and judges, and through them anyone who lives among neighbors, rivals and enemies
settings.when: Collected under Hezekiah; the sayings themselves may be older
settings.why: To teach a young courtier how to behave before a king (25:6–7), when to go to court and when to settle (25:8–10), how to speak well (25:11–15), and how to treat neighbors and even enemies (25:16–22). The court setting explains why kings and messengers appear so often. It also gives the enemy saying (25:21–22) its edge: at court, rivals were everywhere, and kindness to them was a costly choice.
settings.readers: Once Judah had no court, readers applied the king sayings to anyone with authority, and to God as king. Jesus' advice to take the lowest seat at a feast (Luke 14:8–11) and Paul's use of 25:21–22 (Romans 12:20) carried the court's lessons on humility and enemies into synagogue and church.
views: Bryce and Van Leeuwen see 25:2–27 as a deliberately framed instruction for courtiers.
Others see a looser string of sayings joined by catchwords and images.

title: Fools, Idlers and Smooth Talkers
sum: Chapter 26 is the most tightly organized chapter in Proverbs. Twelve sayings on the fool (26:1–12) are followed by four on the lazy one (26:13–16) and a dozen on troublemakers with words: the meddler, the joker who deceives, the gossip, the quarrelsome man, and the smooth-talking hater (26:17–28). Nearly every saying is a picture, and many are comic: a lame man's dangling legs, a lion in the town square, a man too lazy to lift his hand from the bowl.

At the center of the fool series stand two sayings that seem to contradict each other: "Don't answer a fool in line with his folly" and "Answer a fool in line with his folly" (26:4–5). The pair is deliberate. It shows that wisdom is not a rulebook but judgment: knowing which proverb fits which moment. The chapter also contains the saying about the dog that returns to its vomit (26:11), which 2 Peter 2:22 applies to people who turn back from the faith.
readings: Read as satire
The fool, the lazy one and the smooth talker are drawn as cartoons. The humor makes the lesson stick, and it lets a young reader laugh at the fool before he finds the fool in himself (26:12).
Read as a lesson in reading proverbs

26:4–5, 26:7 and 26:9 are about how proverbs work. A proverb in a fool's mouth is useless or dangerous, and two true proverbs can point in opposite directions. The chapter teaches how to use the whole book.

views.H: The pictures come from village and town life: snow, rain, birds, horses and donkeys, slings, thorns, dogs, doors on pivot stones, shared bowls, charcoal fires, glazed pots. A fool sent as a messenger (26:6) and hired workers (26:10) reflect the households and courts where these sayings were used.
views.C: Scholars such as Van Leeuwen treat 26:1–12 as a carefully built unit, a "proverb poem" on the fool, linked by the word kesil in every verse except 26:2. The Greek translator kept 26:4–5 but expanded 26:11 and rendered 26:10 very differently. Several verses (26:7, 10, 23) are among the hardest in the book, and modern versions differ on them.
views.W: Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom also mocks the fool and the lazy, and warns against the hot-tempered and the talebearer (Amenemope, Ptahhotep). The sow saying that 2 Peter pairs with 26:11 has a close relative in the Syriac Story of Ahiqar.
views.J: The Talmud (Shabbat 30b) says the sages almost withdrew Proverbs from use because 26:4 and 26:5 contradict each other, and solved it by applying one to matters of Torah and the other to worldly matters.
views.X: 2 Peter 2:22 applies 26:11 to false teachers who return to their old ways. Paul's "fool's speech" in 2 Corinthians 11–12, where he answers boasters by boasting "as a fool", is often read as a use of 26:5. Christian moral teachers used 26:12 against spiritual pride.

deep.h: Answer a fool, do not answer a fool (26:4–5)
deep.b:
No one put these sayings side by side by accident. Both use the same words: "answer", "a fool", "in line with his folly". Both give a reason: one to protect you ("or you too will become like him"), one to protect the fool and those around him ("or he will be wise in his own eyes").

Readers have resolved the tension in three main ways. Two subjects: the Talmud (Shabbat 30b) says "Answer" applies to matters of Torah, where an error must be corrected, and "Do not answer" to worldly matters; its example is Rabban Gamaliel answering a student who mocked his teaching. Two manners: the little word ke-, "in line with", can mean "in the same way as" or "as it deserves". Do not answer in the fool's style, with insults and shouting; but do answer his folly as it deserves, by exposing it. Two situations: most modern commentators, among them Kidner, Fox and Waltke, think the pair teaches that no proverb works everywhere. Sometimes silence protects you; sometimes silence lets the fool win. Wisdom is knowing which time it is.

The Greek translator kept the pair unchanged. Paul seems to follow 26:5 when he answers the boasting "super-apostles" in their own terms, "as a fool", while saying he hates to do it (2 Corinthians 11:16–12:11). The same sense of timing runs through Ecclesiastes 3:7: "a time to keep quiet and a time to speak".

deep.h: The dog and its vomit, from Proverbs to 2 Peter
deep.b:
26:11 is the only saying from Proverbs' fool series that the New Testament quotes. 2 Peter 2:20–22 describes people who escaped the world's corruption through knowing Christ, then were entangled again; it would have been better for them never to have known the way. "The true proverb" has come true for them: a dog turns back to its own vomit, and a washed sow goes back to rolling in the mud.

Two facts stand out when the Greek is checked. First, 2 Peter does not use the Greek of Proverbs: the Greek translation has emetos for vomit and a different verb, while 2 Peter has exerama. Second, the sow saying is not in the Bible at all. A close relative appears in the Syriac Story of Ahiqar, where a son is compared to a pig that went to the baths and then wallowed in mud. So 2 Peter seems to quote two proverbs current in his day, one of which goes back to Proverbs 26:11. Christians have used the verse in teaching about repentance and backsliding; how it bears on whether a true believer can finally fall away is part of a wider debate (see perseverance).

echoes: 22:13; 19:24; 18:8; 6:16–19; 1 Samuel 12:17–18; Psalm 7:15–16; Psalm 57:6; Ecclesiastes 10:8; Ecclesiastes 3:7; 2 Corinthians 11:16–12:11; 2 Peter 2:22; James 3:5–6

settings.what: Sayings on the fool, the lazy one and the troublemaker
settings.by: The sages, as collected by Hezekiah's scribes
settings.to: Young men at court or in a scribal school, learning how to recognize and deal with fools, idlers, gossips and liars, and how not to become one
settings.when: Collected under Hezekiah (25:1); the sayings are older and from many hands
settings.why: To give a young man a set of portraits he can recognize in others and in himself: the fool who must be handled with care (26:1–12), the lazy one who is sure he is wise (26:13–16), and the people who do harm with words (26:17–28). The comic pictures make the warnings memorable. For hearers expected to send messengers, hire workers and settle disputes, knowing how to deal with a fool was a practical skill.
settings.readers: Rabbinic readers turned the pair 26:4–5 into a rule about when to argue Torah (Shabbat 30b), and 2 Peter 2:22 applied the dog of 26:11 to those who turn back from the faith. Moralists in both traditions used the lazy one and the gossip of 26:13–22 as stock warnings in teaching the young.

title: Friends, Flattery and the Flock
sum: Chapter 27 is about relationships: boasting and praise (27:1–2), anger and jealousy (27:3–4), honest friends and kissing enemies (27:5–6), neighbors near and brothers far away (27:10), a teacher and his son (27:11), quarrelsome wives (27:15–16), and the famous saying, "Iron is sharpened by iron, / and a person sharpens his friend's face" (27:17). A face reflected in water (27:19) and the never-full eyes of human beings (27:20) look inward.

The chapter ends with a short poem, the only extended poem in Hezekiah's collection (27:23–27): know your flocks, because wealth and even a crown do not last, but a well-kept flock renews itself every year. It may be advice to a farmer or a reminder to a ruler that he is a shepherd.
readings: Read as practical advice

Most of these sayings need no allegory. They tell a young man how to keep friends, avoid flatterers, choose his words, and run a household that will last. The herd poem says the same about wealth: tend what is living and renewable.
Read as royal instruction
Read with 25:2–7, the crown of 27:24 and the shepherd image of 27:23 turn the poem into advice for kings, whose power depends on caring for their people, a theme the prophets develop (Ezekiel 34).

views.H: The chapter shows an agricultural household: flocks and herds, goats sold to buy fields, milk for the family and the servant girls, fig trees tended for years, grain pounded in a mortar. Pledges taken for debts (27:13) and loud greetings at dawn (27:14) reflect village life.
views.C: 27:12 and 27:13 repeat 22:3 and 20:16, and 27:15 belongs with 19:13 and 21:9. Van Leeuwen sees 27:23–27 as a closing piece for chapters 25–27. Several verses are textually hard (27:9, 16, 19), and the Greek adds lines at 27:20 and 27:21.
views.W: Friendship, flattery and the shepherd-king are common themes in ancient Near Eastern wisdom. Kings in Mesopotamia and Egypt called themselves shepherds of their people, which supports a royal reading of 27:23–27.
views.J: The Talmud applies 27:17 to two scholars who sharpen each other in the study of law (Taanit 7a), and the saying became a motto for the Jewish practice of studying in pairs.
views.X: Christian readers heard the "kisses from someone who hates you" of 27:6 in Judas' kiss (Matthew 26:48–49), and James' warning against boasting about tomorrow echoes 27:1 (James 4:13–16). "Iron sharpens iron" is widely used for mutual encouragement among believers.

deep.b:
Few proverbs are quoted more today. The usual sense is friends who make each other better: honest talk, accountability, mentoring. The Hebrew supports more than one reading. Yachad, "sharpen", is used of swords and of tongues sharpened to wound (Ezekiel 21:9–11; Psalm 57:4). Sharpening iron with iron is friction, sparks and wear. The "face" of a friend (penei re'ehu) is his presence, expression and spirit.

So the saying may mean that friends improve one another by honest friction (the reading of 27:5–6: "A rebuke brought into the open is better / than love that stays out of sight"); or simply that people shape one another, for better or worse, by contact (compare 13:20; 22:24–25). The Talmud's use of the verse for two scholars debating Torah keeps the friction in view (Taanit 7a). The popular reading is fair to the verse, as long as it remembers that sharpening is not always comfortable.

The poem moves from command (know your flock, 27:23) to reason (wealth and crowns do not last, 27:24) to promise (the grass returns every year, and the flock provides clothing, land and milk, 27:25–27). It contrasts two kinds of wealth: chosen, stored riches that can be lost, and living wealth that renews itself with care. It ends with the word "life" (27:27).

The mention of a crown (nezer) suggests that the poem had a royal reader in view as well as a farmer, as one would expect in a collection made at Hezekiah's court. Israel's kings were meant to shepherd the people (2 Samuel 5:2), and Ezekiel condemns shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock (Ezekiel 34:1–10). Jesus, the good shepherd, knows his own sheep by name (John 10:3, 14).

settings.what: Sayings on friends, enemies, praise and the inner life
settings.by: The sages, with one saying in the voice of a father or teacher (27:11)
settings.to: Young men learning to live among friends, neighbors, rivals and family; 27:11 speaks directly to "my son"
settings.why: To help a young man judge people well: to tell a true friend from a flatterer (27:5–6, 14), keep old friendships (27:10), avoid foolish guarantees (27:13), and know himself (27:19–21). The father's appeal in 27:11 shows the setting: a teacher's honor rests on the pupil's wisdom. The sayings about the quarrelsome wife (27:15–16) speak to the young man as a future husband.
settings.readers: Later readers drew the friendship sayings into communal life: the Talmud applied "iron sharpens iron" to two scholars studying together (Taanit 7a), and Christians heard the "kisses from someone who hates you" (27:6) in Judas' kiss. James' warning against boasting about tomorrow echoes 27:1 (James 4:13–16).

settings.to: A landowner or head of a household with flocks and herds; possibly a king or official, given the crown of 27:24
settings.why: To urge steady, personal care of living wealth instead of trust in stored riches or status. For a farmer, it is advice about keeping a household fed and clothed. For a ruler, it is a reminder that a crown passes away, while a well-shepherded people sustains the kingdom.
settings.readers: Synagogue and church readers often took the herdsman's poem as a picture of leadership: rulers and teachers must know the condition of their flock, as the good shepherd knows his sheep (John 10:3, 14). Others kept its plain sense as advice on caring for living, renewable wealth instead of trusting stored riches.
views: Advice to a landowner about tending flocks (most commentators).
A shepherd-king poem for rulers, closing the court collection of 25–27 (Van Leeuwen, Malchow and others).

title: When the Wicked Rise
sum: The tone of the collection changes in chapter 28. Most sayings now set two kinds of people against each other: the wicked who flee when no one is chasing and the righteous who feel as safe as a lion (28:1); those who abandon the law and those who keep it (28:4); the crooked rich and the honest poor (28:6). Four sayings on what happens "when the wicked rise" and "when the righteous" prosper (28:12, 28; 29:2, 16) run through chapters 28–29 like a refrain.

Rulers are everywhere: a land with many princes (28:2), a wicked ruler like a roaring lion (28:15), a ruler who oppresses (28:16). So is money: interest taken from the poor will pass to someone kind to the poor (28:8), and those who hurry to get rich will be punished (28:20, 22). At the center is one of the Bible's clearest sayings about confession: "The one who hides his offenses will not get ahead, / but the one who admits them and turns from them will receive mercy" (28:13).
readings: Read as a manual for rulers

Bruce Malchow argued that chapters 28–29 are "a manual for future monarchs": the refrain sayings show how a ruler's character affects a whole people, and many sayings concern justice, bribes, the poor and the law.
Read as wisdom for everyone

The same sayings apply to anyone with power over others: parents, employers, lenders, judges. The righteous and the wicked are not classes but choices, and the law (28:4, 7, 9) is the standard for all.

views.H: Hezekiah's court remembered the northern kingdom's quick turnover of kings (28:2) and the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Debt and interest were real threats to poor farmers in Judah, as the prophets of the 700s show (Amos 2:6–8; Micah 2:1–2).
views.C: Scholars note that 28–29 differ from 25–27: fewer comparisons, more contrasts, and more religious language (the LORD, the law, prayer). Some see a deliberate structure built on the refrain sayings (Malchow); others think 28–29 were a separate collection joined to 25–27. 28:6 and 28:19 repeat 19:1 and 12:11.
views.W: Instruction for future rulers is a known ancient genre, such as the Egyptian Instruction for Merikare and the Mesopotamian Advice to a Prince. Like them, 28–29 warn against oppression and bribes; unlike them, they tie justice to the LORD and his law.
views.J: The word torah in 28:4, 7, 9 has always been read in Jewish tradition as the Torah. The Talmud uses 28:13 in teaching how to confess (Yoma 86b), and the laws of interest draw on 28:8.
views.X: Christians read 28:13 with 1 John 1:9 and Psalm 32, and 28:8 shaped the medieval church's long debate about interest. Different churches have answered the question of interest differently (see below).

deep.b:
The verse names two kinds of profit on a loan: neshekh, "bite", and tarbit, "increase". The same pair appears in the law: "Do not take interest or profit from him" (Leviticus 25:36). Israel's law forbade charging a fellow Israelite interest (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19–20), and Psalm 15 counts lending without interest as a mark of the person who may stand in God's presence (Psalm 15:5). The loans in view were mostly to neighbors in need: seed after a bad harvest, food in a famine. Nehemiah 5 shows how such debts could drive families into slavery.

Proverbs adds no new law. It makes a prediction: wealth grown by interest on the poor will pass to "someone who is kind to the poor". It does not say how, and it trusts that God will move such gains to others (13:22; Job 27:16–17).

Later readers applied the verse widely. The Talmud discusses it in its laws of interest, and Jewish law later developed the partnership contract (heter iska) for business lending. In Christian history, councils of the medieval church condemned usurers, while the Reformers Luther and Calvin argued over whether moderate interest on business loans was lawful. Today most churches accept fair interest in commerce and condemn lending that exploits the poor, but they reached that position by different routes.
deep.refs: 28:8; Leviticus 25:35–37; Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Psalm 15:5; Nehemiah 5:1–13; Ezekiel 18:8; Luke 6:34–35

traditions.q: 28:8 says wealth made from interest will pass to someone kind to the poor. Is it wrong for Christians to charge or earn interest?
views: The medieval Church forbade usury, meaning any profit on a loan as such; the Third Lateran Council (1179) denied Christian burial to open usurers. Later teaching accepted interest on loans where money is used productively, and today the Catechism condemns "usurious and avaricious dealings" that harm the poor rather than all interest (Catechism 2269).

The canons forbid clergy to lend at interest (Council of Nicaea, canon 17), and Fathers such as Basil of Caesarea preached against usurers. Orthodox churches today generally accept ordinary banking for laypeople while upholding the Fathers' condemnation of exploiting the needy.
Luther attacked high interest and usury sharply (Trade and Usury, 1524), while allowing limited rates under civil law; later Lutheranism accepted moderate interest.
Calvin argued that the law of Moses forbade interest that oppresses the poor, not all interest on business loans; moderate interest is lawful if it is fair and the needy are still lent to freely.

echoes: Leviticus 26:17; Leviticus 26:36; Leviticus 25:36; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Psalm 15:5; Deuteronomy 1:17; Deuteronomy 21:20; Psalm 32:1–5; 1 John 1:9; Ezekiel 22:25; Mark 7:9–13; Matthew 25:31–46; 19:1; 12:11; 24:23

settings.what: Contrasts of the righteous and the wicked, with sayings for rulers
settings.by: The sages, as collected by Hezekiah's scribes
settings.to: Young men of the court and the families of Judah's leaders, who would one day judge, lend, rule and advise
settings.when: Collected under Hezekiah (25:1), in a kingdom that had seen the northern kingdom collapse
settings.why: To show that a ruler's or a leader's character shapes a whole people (28:2, 12, 15–16, 28), to bind justice to the law and to the LORD (28:4–5, 9), and to warn the powerful against exploiting the poor through interest, bribes and favoritism (28:3, 8, 21). Knowing the audience explains why so many sayings are about rulers and money.
settings.readers: In the Middle Ages 28:8 was cited in the long debate about usury, and churches and Jewish law reached different answers on lending at interest. 28:13 became a key text on confession in both traditions (Yoma 86b; 1 John 1:9).
views: Chapters 28–29 were shaped for future kings and officials (Malchow).
The sayings address every Israelite, with rulers as one group among many (most commentators).

title: The Rod and the Vision
sum: The last chapter of Hezekiah's collection continues the contrasts of chapter 28: the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, the just king and the greedy one. It warns the stiff-necked (29:1), praises the king who judges the poor faithfully (29:14), and reminds rulers and their courts that justice finally comes from the LORD (29:26).

Two sayings from this chapter are among the most quoted in Proverbs. "Rod and rebuke give wisdom" (29:15) is one of the rod sayings that shaped centuries of child-rearing. "Where no vision is given, a people runs wild" (29:18) is often misquoted as a call for goals and plans, but it speaks of prophetic revelation and of keeping God's law. The collection ends where it began, with a stark division: the righteous and the wicked find each other abhorrent (29:27).
readings: Read as household and court wisdom

Discipline of sons (29:15, 17) and slaves (29:19, 21) sits beside advice for kings (29:4, 12, 14). In the ancient world the household and the kingdom were run on the same model, and the sayings move easily between them.
Read as the end of a book

The chapter gathers the themes of 25–29: the king, the fool, the poor, anger, pride and humility. Its last verses (29:25–27) turn from human rulers to the LORD, who gives justice, and set the two ways side by side one last time.

views.H: Fathers, mothers, slaves and servants, kings and their officials all appear. Slavery and physical punishment were normal parts of household life in Israel and its neighbors, and the law regulated both (Exodus 21:20–21; Deuteronomy 21:18–21; Deuteronomy 25:1–3).
views.C: 29:1 echoes 6:15, 29:13 echoes 22:2, and 29:22 echoes 15:18. 29:18 is unusual for mentioning prophetic vision and law together, and some scholars think it reflects the influence of the prophetic movement in Hezekiah's time (Isaiah and Micah) or a later editor. In the Greek, 31:10–31 follows straight after 29:27.
views.W: The rod in education appears across ancient wisdom: a Late Egyptian school text (Papyrus Anastasi III, as reported by Caminos) says a boy's ear is on his back, and the Words of Ahiqar tell a father not to spare the rod. What is distinctive in Proverbs is the claim that the rod and the rebuke "give wisdom", and the warning against neglect (29:15b).
views.J: Rabbinic law kept 29:15 and 29:17 but limited physical discipline: "only with a shoelace" (Bava Batra 21a), never a grown son (Moed Katan 17a). 29:18 was read as a description of times without prophecy, and the last line as praise for the one who keeps the Torah.
views.X: Christians have used 29:15 and 29:17 with 13:24 and 23:13–14 to defend physical discipline; others read them in light of Ephesians 6:4 and the gospel's direction toward gentleness. 29:23 is echoed in Jesus' teaching that the humble will be exalted (Luke 14:11).

deep.b:
What the Hebrew says. Shevet is a wooden rod or stick: a shepherd's club, a ruler's scepter, a stick for beating a slave or a criminal (Psalm 23:4; Genesis 49:10; Exodus 21:20; 26:3). In Proverbs it is used on children (13:24; 22:15; 23:13–14; 29:15). The Plain English Translation does not soften it: this is physical punishment. But the verse joins the rod to tokhachat, rebuke in words, and names the goal: wisdom. The second line is as important as the first: a boy "left to run loose" (meshullach, turned out like an animal let loose) brings his mother shame. The saying warns against neglect as much as it commends punishment.

How it was used. Ancient schools in Egypt and Mesopotamia beat pupils, and Israel's scribal training likely did too. Through most of Jewish and Christian history the verse was taken as a plain endorsement of physical discipline, at home and in school.

How it is read today. Jewish law limited the rod early: the Talmud allows a teacher to strike a child only with a shoelace (Bava Batra 21a) and bans a father who strikes an adult son (Moed Katan 17a); Maimonides forbids cruel blows and sticks. Many Orthodox and most liberal Jewish educators now reject striking children. Among Christians, many conservative Protestants (James Dobson's Dare to Discipline, 1970) teach that measured spanking, given in love and self-control, follows these sayings. Others argue that the sayings describe the ancient practice of beating with a stick, often of older youths, with no limits, so that no one actually applies them literally; William Webb reads the Bible as moving toward gentler discipline, and many Catholic, Orthodox and mainline teachers stress Ephesians 6:4 and the dignity of the child. Churches differ in what their teachers recommend more than in official doctrine; see 13:24 for the first rod saying.

In the KJV the verse reads "Where there is no vision, the people perish", and it is often quoted to mean that people and organizations need a vision for the future. The Hebrew says something different. Chazon is a revelation from God through a prophet: when Samuel was a boy, "The LORD's word was rare in those days; no vision was breaking out" (1 Samuel 3:1). And the people do not "perish" but yippara', "run wild", the word used when Israel ran wild at the golden calf (Exodus 32:25).

Read in Hebrew, the verse says that a people without God's word loses all restraint, and the person who keeps God's law is happy. It joins the prophets' word and Moses' law, as Hezekiah's age did: Isaiah and Micah prophesied in his reign, and the king restored the worship the law commanded. The Greek has "There will be no interpreter for a lawless nation, but the one who keeps the law is blessed."

echoes: 6:15; 22:2; 15:18; 13:24; 22:15; 23:13–14; Exodus 32:9; Exodus 32:25; 1 Samuel 3:1; Leviticus 5:1; Psalm 72:1–4; Isaiah 11:4; Luke 14:11; Luke 15:30; Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:11

settings.what: Last sayings of the Hezekiah collection
settings.by: The sages; 29:17 speaks to a parent ("your son")
settings.to: Young men of the court and heads of households: future fathers, masters, judges and royal officials
settings.why: To finish the collection's training in character and rule: how to raise a son (29:15, 17), manage a household (29:19, 21), judge the poor (29:7, 14), control anger (29:8, 11, 22), resist fear of people (29:25) and remember that justice comes from the LORD (29:26). The rod sayings were advice to fathers in a world where beating was normal; knowing that helps readers see both what the text says and what it was trying to prevent: a child left without guidance.
settings.readers: In the Second Temple period, when many felt that prophecy had ceased, 29:18 read as a description of their own age, with the Torah left to guide the people. The rod sayings of 29:15 and 29:17 shaped Jewish and Christian child-rearing for centuries, and their use is still debated today.
